unit: Replace one engine water (coolant) pump that is mounted outside the engine and driven by the accessory (serpentine) belt, or is electric (the BMW example). Covers the pump (with its gasket where the listing includes one) and the labor to swap it, including refilling the cooling system where the source's time includes it. Not included: a pump driven by the timing belt or timing chain (a much bigger job, normally quoted together with the timing belt; see the finding and extras), thermostat, drive belt, coolant, diagnosis, shop supplies and tax.

finding: The live range of $380-$1,475 is about right, and it is wide because it spans two different jobs: an external pump driven by the accessory belt (what the four examples here price), and a pump buried behind the timing belt. Built totals (pump + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2013 Chevrolet Cruze 1.4L about $247-$663 (1.6-2.0 hr); midsize 2016 Honda Accord 2.4L about $224-$497 (1.4-2.0 hr); truck 2014 Ford F-150 5.0L about $219-$518 (1.0-2.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i (electric pump) about $569-$944 (1.0-2.0 hr). The low ends fall under the live floor of $380, but that is not evidence the floor is too high: they price the pump alone at online prices ($55-$99 for the three belt-driven examples) with no coolant, thermostat or belt, and they use warranty or seller times, which are the least a shop bills. Every outside estimate starts at $353 or more, and RepairPal's parts figure alone is $525-$598. How solid the labor times are: the low end of every class is now a time stated for the example vehicle itself. Two are manufacturer warranty times: GM's 1.6 hr for the 2011-2014 Cruze 1.4L (1.3 hr plus 0.3 hr to fill the cooling system) and Honda's 1.4 hr for the 2013-2016 Accord 4-cylinder (the same bulletin gives 1.7-1.8 hr for the CR-V). The truck low end is weaker: a parts seller's approximate 1 hour for the 2011-2014 F-150 5.0L, not a Ford time. The luxury figure is a parts seller's 'hour or two' do-it-yourself estimate for the same BMW engine; as a cross-check, Acura's warranty time for a belt-driven pump on the 2015-16 TLX 2.4L is 1.2 hr. The high end for the three belt-driven classes is still one general statement ('one or two hours') from a how-to guide, not a book time and not vehicle-specific; outside estimators assume 2-4 hours, so real quotes will often run above our totals. The examples were changed from the Corolla, Camry and 2016 F-150 because no manufacturer time was found for those; parts prices were re-sourced for the new examples. Top of the range: none of the four examples has a pump driven by the timing belt. As a sourced check on that kind of job, Honda's recall bulletin 19-045 allows 3.1-3.4 hr to inspect and replace the timing belt on the 3.5L V6 (2019 Odyssey 3.1, 2018-2019 Pilot 3.2, 2019 Ridgeline 3.4); the pump sits behind that belt, the bulletin does not include changing it, and the allowance covers no coolant drain and refill, so the true pump job is longer. An Aisin TKH-002 timing belt kit with water pump for the Pilot and Odyssey was $282.99 (one retailer only; list $448.42). That builds to roughly $655-$827 as a floor for a timing-belt-and-pump job with aftermarket parts, comfortably inside the live ceiling; with dealer parts, a longer real-world labor time and a higher labor rate the $1,475 top is plausible, but we could not build a total that high from stated figures, so the ceiling is supported by the outside estimates (which cite 4-8 hours for these engines) rather than proven. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): kept at low confidence because the truck time is a parts seller's estimate and every belt-driven high end is one general how-to statement.
extras: A quote often adds coolant and a cooling system bleed or pressure test, a thermostat, a drive belt, new pump bolts or gaskets, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies, coolant disposal, and sales tax. On engines where the timing belt drives the pump, shops normally quote the timing belt, tensioner and idlers in the same job, which raises the total a lot. The parts figures here are the pump (with its gasket where included) only. Sourced example of that bigger job: on Honda's 3.5L V6 the maker's own warranty allowance just to replace the timing belt is 3.1-3.4 hours (recall bulletin 19-045), and an aftermarket timing belt kit that includes the water pump was $282.99 at one retailer (Aisin TKH-002, Pilot and Odyssey).
